after.claim: Direct calculation gives $\det(A-\lambda B)=1-\lambda$, a nonzero polynomial, so the pencil is regular although $\det B=0$.

The homogeneous determinant is $\det(\beta A-\alpha B)=\det\begin{pmatrix}\beta-\alpha&0\\0&\beta\end{pmatrix} =\beta(\beta-\alpha).$ Its projective roots are $[1:1]$, the finite eigenvalue $1$, and $[1:0]$, the infinite eigenvalue.
For $(A,B)=(I_2,0)$, $\det(A-\lambda B)=\det I_2=1$, so the pencil is regular. Its homogeneous determinant is $\det(\beta I_2)=\beta^2$, which vanishes only at $[1:0]$, the infinite eigenvalue pair.
For $(A,B)=(\operatorname{diag}(1,0),0)$, $\det(A-\lambda B)=\det A=0$ for every $\lambda$, so the determinant polynomial is identically zero and the pencil is singular.

The matrix $M$ is positive definite because $u^TMu=2u_1^2+u_2^2>0$ for $u\ne0$. Also $u^TKu=2u_1^2+2(u_1-u_2)^2+u_2^2>0$ for $u\ne0$. The determinant polynomial is $\det(K-\lambda M)=(4-2\lambda)(3-\lambda)-4 =2(\lambda-1)(\lambda-4),$ so the pencil is regular and its eigenvalues are $1,4$.

For $x_1=(1,1)^T$, $Kx_1=(2,1)^T=Mx_1$. For $x_2=(1,-2)^T$, $Kx_2=(8,-8)^T=4Mx_2$. Their mass inner product is $x_1^TMx_2=2-2=0$. Thus they are distinct generalized eigenmodes and are $M$-orthogonal; [F1] gives the general real-spectrum and orthogonal-basis conclusion for this pencil.

For $x=e_1$ and $\mu=2$, the residual is $r=Kx-\mu Mx=(0,-2)^T$. Hence $\|x\|_M=\sqrt2$ and, since $M^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)$, $\|r\|_{M^{-1}}=2$. The theorem [F2] therefore bounds the distance from $2$ to $\{1,4\}$ by $2/\sqrt2=\sqrt2$; indeed that distance is $1$.

Let $N\ge2$, $h>0$, $k>0$, and $t_n=nk$. For the finite periodic grid put $J_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ and reduce every shifted index modulo $N$. A periodic grid function is a map $v:J_N\to\mathbb C$, with weighted norm

The infinite uniform grid has indices $j\in\mathbb Z$ and positions $x_j=jh$. On the periodic and infinite grids define
$$ (D_+v)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-v_j}{h},\qquad (D_-v)_j=\frac{v_j-v_{j-1}}{h},\qquad (D_0v)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-v_{j-1}}{2h},\qquad (\Delta_hv)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-2v_j+v_{j-1}}{h^2}. $$
Use the inner product linear in its first entry,
$$ \langle p,q\rangle_{2,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}p_j\overline{q_j},\qquad \langle D_+p,D_+q\rangle_{e,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(D_+p)_j\overline{(D_+q)_j}, $$
where the indices in $D_+$ are reduced periodically, and set $\|D_+p\|_{e,h}^2=\langle D_+p,D_+p\rangle_{e,h}$. The same definitions apply to real-valued grid functions.

For a finite interval of length $L=Nh$, use physical nodes $x_j=jh$ with indices $j=0,\ldots,N$. On its edges $j=0,\ldots,N-1$ define $(D_+v)_j=(v_{j+1}-v_j)/h$, and on interior nodes $j=1,\ldots,N-1$ use $(\Delta_hv)_j=(v_{j+1}-2v_j+v_{j-1})/h^2$. At the right endpoint define $(D_-v)_N=(v_N-v_{N-1})/h$. The interior inner product, norm, and edge inner product are
$$ \langle p,q\rangle_h=h\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}p_j\overline{q_j},\qquad \|v\|_h^2=\langle v,v\rangle_h,\qquad \langle p,q\rangle_{e,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(D_+p)_j\overline{(D_+q)_j}. $$
Dirichlet grid functions have prescribed endpoint values; when they are zero, the interior norm and edge inner product above are the ones used for the wave energy.

after.claim: If $a<0$, set $A=-a>0$ and $\widetilde u(x,t)=u(-x,t)$. For fixed $x$, its time difference quotient is that of $u$ at $(-x,t)$, so $\widetilde u_t(x,t)=u_t(-x,t)$. In its spatial difference quotient, substitute $s=-h$ to get $\widetilde u_x(x,t)=-u_x(-x,t)$. Repeating these coordinate calculations gives $\partial_x^p\partial_t^q\widetilde u(x,t)=(-1)^p(\partial_x^p\partial_t^q u)(-x,t)$, so the period and derivative bounds are preserved. The PDE gives $\widetilde u_t+A\widetilde u_x=u_t(-x,t)-A u_x(-x,t)=0$. The definition's reflection $j\mapsto-j$ identifies each negative-speed stencil residual with the corresponding positive-speed residual of $\widetilde u$ at the reflected point. If $a>0$, take $A=a$ and $\widetilde u=u$. It is therefore enough to derive the estimates for positive speed $A$.

For this positive-speed solution, differentiating $\widetilde u_t=-A\widetilde u_x$ in $t$ and $x$, then using [F4] to commute the order-two mixed partials, gives $\widetilde u_{tt}=-A\widetilde u_{xt}=-A\widetilde u_{tx}=A^2\widetilde u_{xx}$. Differentiating this identity in $t$ and the PDE twice in $x$, then using [F4] to commute the order-three partials, gives $\widetilde u_{ttt}=A^2\widetilde u_{xxt}=A^2\widetilde u_{txx}=-A^3\widetilde u_{xxx}$. By [F3] these derivatives exist, and the bounded derivatives in the hypotheses make the Taylor remainders uniform. Taylor's formula from [F2] yields $$ \frac{\widetilde u(x,t+k)-\widetilde u(x,t)}{k}=\widetilde u_t+\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+\frac{k^2}{6}\widetilde u_{ttt}+O(k^3), $$ $$ \frac{\widetilde u(x+h,t)-\widetilde u(x-h,t)}{2h}=\widetilde u_x+\frac{h^2}{6}\widetilde u_{xxx}+O(h^4),\qquad \frac{\widetilde u(x+h,t)-2\widetilde u(x,t)+\widetilde u(x-h,t)}{h^2}=\widetilde u_{xx}+\frac{h^2}{12}\widetilde u_{xxxx}+O(h^4). $$ The one-sided expansions are $(\widetilde u(x,t)-\widetilde u(x-h,t))/h=\widetilde u_x-\frac h2\widetilde u_{xx}+O(h^2)$ and $(\widetilde u(x+h,t)-\widetilde u(x,t))/h=\widetilde u_x+\frac h2\widetilde u_{xx}+O(h^2)$.

Substituting the step 2.1 expansions into [F1] with speed $A=|a|$ and using $\widetilde u_t+A\widetilde u_x=0$ gives $$ \tau_{\rm up}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}-\frac{Ah}{2}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2),\quad \tau_{\rm down}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+\frac{Ah}{2}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2),\quad \tau_{\rm centered}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+O(k^2+h^2). $$ For Lax--Friedrichs the symmetric average contributes $-h^2\widetilde u_{xx}/(2k)$ to the residual, so $\tau_{\rm LF}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}-\frac{h^2}{2k}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2+h^4/k)$. For Lax--Wendroff the $k\widetilde u_{tt}/2$ term cancels the second-difference term by $\widetilde u_{tt}=A^2\widetilde u_{xx}$, leaving $\tau_{\rm LW}=\frac{k^2}{6}\widetilde u_{ttt}+\frac{Ah^2}{6}\widetilde u_{xxx}+O(k^3+h^4+kh^2)$. Reflection in step 1.1 transfers these residual bounds to the negative-speed branch.

The mesh ratio bounds imply $k=O(h)$ and $h^2/k=O(h)$. Thus the first four residuals are uniformly $O(h)$, and every displayed Lax--Wendroff term is $O(h^2)$ or smaller. By step 1.1 the same estimates hold for either velocity sign. The conclusion concerns only the sampled smooth solution in the stated periodic setting.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. $$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Let $k\ge2$. If $f\in C^k(U)$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, then every iterated derivative of $f$ of order $k$ is unchanged by any permutation of its coordinate differentiations.

**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

The explicit function $u^*(y,s)=u_0(y-as)$ has partial derivatives $u^*_y=u_0'(y-as)$ and $u^*_s=-a u_0'(y-as)$ by one-variable difference quotients, so it solves $u_t+a u_x=0$ with initial data $u_0$.
To verify uniqueness, let $u$ be any classical solution on an open neighborhood of this characteristic segment with the same initial data, fix $(x,t)$, and set $v(s)=u(x+a(s-t),s)$ on $[0,t]$.
For interior $s$ and small nonzero $\delta$ whose coordinate segments remain in the solution domain, applying [F6] separately in the first and second coordinates gives $$\frac{v(s+\delta)-v(s)}{\delta}=a u_x(\xi_\delta,s+\delta)+u_t(x+a(s-t),\eta_\delta),$$ where $\xi_\delta$ lies between $x+a(s-t)$ and $x+a(s+\delta-t)$, and $\eta_\delta$ lies between $s$ and $s+\delta$.
As $\delta\to0$, these intermediate points tend to $(x+a(s-t),s)$, so continuity of the partials in [F2] yields $v'(s)=a u_x(x+a(s-t),s)+u_t(x+a(s-t),s)=0$.
Then [F6] makes $v$ constant, hence $u(x,t)=u_0(x-at)$. Since $0\le T-n_mk_m<k_m$ and $k_m\to0$, the exact characteristic foot $j_mh_m-a n_mk_m$ tends to $aT-aT=0$. By continuity and $u_0(0)=1$, the exact sample tends to $1$, while step 2.1 gives numerical value zero. Thus the sampled maximum error does not tend to zero.
On N_q=4q grids at nu=1/2, the z=i mode forces unbounded power norms within each fixed time interval.

after.claim: Put $R=aT\varepsilon/(4(1+\varepsilon))$ and take $\chi$ from [F4]. Set $u_0(x)=\chi(3x/R)$. Then $u_0$ is smooth, equals $1$ at zero, and is supported in $[-2R/3,2R/3]$, a compact subset of $(-R,R)$; by [F8] it is an admissible real-valued datum.

By finite induction [F3], the value at index $j$ after zero steps depends only on $j$. If every value after $n$ steps depends only on initial indices $j-n,\ldots,j+n$, then the next update reads indices $j-1,j,j+1$ at time $n$, whose initial dependence intervals have union $[j-(n+1),j+(n+1)]$. Thus after $n$ steps only initial indices $j-n,\ldots,j+n$ can affect the value.

Along the violating subsequence put $n_m=\lfloor T/k_m\rfloor$ and $j_m=\lfloor aT/h_m+1/2\rfloor$. By [F7], $j_m\le aT/h_m+1/2<j_m+1$, so $|j_mh_m-aT|\le h_m/2$. Since $n_mh_m\le T h_m/k_m\le aT/(1+\varepsilon)$, the left edge of the numerical dependence interval obeys $$ j_mh_m-n_mh_m\ge\frac{aT\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}-\frac{h_m}{2}. $$ For all sufficiently large $m$, this exceeds $R$. Hence every sampled initial value on which $U_{j_m}^{n_m}$ depends is zero, so $U_{j_m}^{n_m}=0$.

For the separate centered-family claim, fix $P>0$ and use $N_q=4q$, $h_q=P/(4q)$, $k_q=h_q/(2a)$, and $r_q=\lfloor T/k_q\rfloor$. Then [F1] gives the centered update with $ak_q/h_q=1/2$, and the Fourier index $\ell=q$ is admissible with $z_\ell=\exp(2\pi i q/(4q))=i$. By [F9] its multiplier is $g=1-i/2$, so $|g|=\sqrt5/2>1$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$ be open and let
$a:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n$, $c:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
The scalar first-order equation

$$u_t(x,t)+a(x,t)\cdot\nabla_x u(x,t)+c(x,t)u(x,t)=f(x,t)$$

is a **linear transport equation**.

Fix $(x_0,t_0)\in\Omega$. A **characteristic through $(x_0,t_0)$** is a
solution $X(\cdot)$ of the ODE

$$X'(s)=a(X(s),s),\qquad X(t_0)=x_0,$$

on an interval containing $t_0$. The corresponding space-time curve is
$s\mapsto (X(s),s)$. If these initial-value problems have unique solutions for
varying initial data, write $X(s;t_0,x_0)$ for the solution through
$(x_0,t_0)$. The resulting maps $x_0\mapsto X(s;t_0,x_0)$, on the domains
where they are defined, form the **characteristic flow** of the transport
field. Without uniqueness there are characteristics, but no single-valued
characteristic flow.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Identify $\mathbb{Z}$ with its canonical copy inside $\mathbb{R}$, along the
embeddings $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$
([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]],
[[def-integers]]). Then for every real $x$ there is **exactly one** integer $m$
with

$$m \;\le\; x \;<\; m + 1 .$$

It is written $\lfloor x \rfloor$ and called the **integer part**, or **floor**,
of $x$.

**Two independent ingredients are needed and neither may be dropped.** Existence
is the Archimedean property ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) together with the
well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]): the first says
that $x$ is caught between two integers at all, the second picks the *least*
integer above $x$. Uniqueness is the discreteness of $\mathbb{Z}$: no integer
lies strictly between $m$ and $m+1$.

This lemma is stated once here and reused. It is what turns "the nearest integer
to $x$" from a picture into an object, and the companion page's oscillator
$\psi(x) = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x - n|$ is computed from it in one line.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Dirichlet grid functions have prescribed endpoint values; when they are zero, the interior norm and edge inner product above are the ones used for the wave energy.

Fix a scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **common-space
linear IVP interface** consists of a Banach space $X$ over $\mathbb K$ and a
strongly continuous semigroup $U(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$, $t\ge0$, as defined in
[[def-strongly-continuous-semigroup]], together with a finite-time bound: for
each $T>0$ there is $M_T<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|U(t)\|\le M_T.$$
The solution with initial value $x\in X$ is $u(t)=U(t)x$. This definition
records the solution operators and their continuous dependence in the same
norm; it makes no claim about a generator domain.

A **consistency subspace** is a dense linear subspace $D\subseteq X$ satisfying
$U(t)D\subseteq D$ for every $t\ge0$. Here dense means
$\overline D^{\,X}=X$, and invariant means the displayed inclusion. It need
not be the domain of a differential generator.

A **common-space time-scheme family** is a sequence of positive time steps
$(\tau_\nu)_{\nu\in\mathbb N}$ with $\tau_\nu\to0$ and bounded linear maps
$S_\nu:X\to X$ in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. Write
$S_\nu^0=I_X$ and recursively set $S_\nu^{n+1}=S_\nu S_\nu^n$ for
$n\in\mathbb N$. All scheme and solution errors below
use the norm of this same space $X$; write $\|\cdot\|$ for that norm and
$\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ for the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm]].

The family is **consistent on $D$** when for every $x\in D$ and $T>0$,
$$\lim_{\nu\to\infty}\max_{\substack{r\in\mathbb N\\r\tau_\nu\le T}}\frac{\|(S_\nu-U(\tau_\nu))U(r\tau_\nu)x\|}{\tau_\nu}=0.$$
The maximum is over a nonempty finite set because it includes $r=0$. This is
the local defect divided by one time step, uniformly over the exact orbit on
the finite time interval.

The family is **stable on finite time intervals** when for every $T>0$ there
is $C_T<\infty$ such that
$$\|S_\nu^n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_T\quad\text{whenever }\nu,n\in\mathbb N\text{ and }n\tau_\nu\le T.$$

$T>0$,
$$\lim_{\nu\to\infty}\max_{\substack{n\in\mathbb N\\n\tau_\nu\le T}}\|S_\nu^n x-U(n\tau_\nu)x\|=0.$$

convergence is the hypothesis used for the reverse implication in the
equivalence theorem below.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

before.claim: If $n=0$, [F3] gives $E=\{0\}$ and the nonempty fixed-point set forces $T(0)=0$; since $w_0=0$, every iterate equals the fixed point. It remains to consider $n\ge1$. before.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

before.claim: If $n=0$, then $E=\{0\}$. If $D$ is empty choose $q=0$; if it is nonempty then $D=\{0\}$, $y=p=T(p)=0$, and $q=0$ satisfies the inequality. Hence assume $n\ge1$. If $D=\varnothing$, any $q$ works. Otherwise consider any finite nonempty list $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in D$ and set $$h_i(q)=\|q-Tp_i\|_2^2-\|y-p_i\|_2^2,\qquad H(q)=\max_{1\le i\le m}h_i(q).$$ The continuous function $H$ is coercive because each $h_i(q)\to+\infty$ as $\|q\|_2\to\infty$. A nonempty sublevel $\{H\le H(0)\}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F2]; [F3] gives a global minimizer $q_0$ of $H$.

Let $I=\{i:h_i(q_0)=H(q_0)\}$ be the nonempty active set. If $0$ were not in the convex hull of the finitely many gradients $2(q_0-Tp_i)$, $i\in I$, project $0$ onto that compact convex hull using [F4]. The projection vector $v\ne0$ obeys $\langle v,2(q_0-Tp_i)\rangle\ge\|v\|_2^2$ for each $i\in I$, by the variational inequality. For sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, every active $h_i(q_0-\epsilon v)$ decreases strictly; the finitely many inactive terms have a strict gap below $H(q_0)$ and remain below it by continuity. This contradicts minimality. Therefore there are weights $\alpha_i\ge0$, supported on $I$, with $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$ and $q_0=\sum_i\alpha_i T p_i$.

Put $\bar p=\sum_i\alpha_i p_i$. Expanding squares and using $q_0=\sum_i\alpha_iTp_i$ gives $$H(q_0)=\sum_i\alpha_i h_i(q_0)=\frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j\|Tp_i-Tp_j\|_2^2-\sum_i\alpha_i\|y-p_i\|_2^2.$$ The nonexpansive hypothesis bounds the double sum by $\frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j\|p_i-p_j\|_2^2=\sum_i\alpha_i\|p_i-\bar p\|_2^2$. The variance identity also gives $\sum_i\alpha_i\|y-p_i\|_2^2=\|y-\bar p\|_2^2+\sum_i\alpha_i\|p_i-\bar p\|_2^2$. Hence $H(q_0)\le-\|y-\bar p\|_2^2\le0$. Thus every finite family of the closed balls $\overline B(Tp,\|y-p\|_2)$ has nonempty intersection.

Choose one $p_0\in D$. The ball $C_0=\overline B(Tp_0,\|y-p_0\|_2)$ is compact by [F2]. The sets $C_0\cap\overline B(Tp,\|y-p\|_2)$ are closed in $C_0$, and every finite intersection is nonempty by step 3.1 applied with $p_0$ included. [F5] therefore supplies a point $q$ in their total intersection, which satisfies every required inequality. The proof used only finite-dimensional compactness and finite convex combinations; no choice principle is invoked.

before.claim: On $|z|=1$, real coefficients give $p^\#(z)=z^n\overline{p(z)}$, so $|p^\#(z)|=|p(z)|$. The strict root hypothesis makes $p$ nonzero on the unit circle, and $|a_0p^\#(z)|<|p(z)|$. Apply [F1] to $p$ and $-a_0p^\#$; $p-a_0p^\#$ has the same $n$ zeros in the disk as $p$.

The polynomial $p-a_0p^\#$ has constant term zero and leading coefficient $1-a_0^2\ne0$, so it is $z$ times a degree-$(n-1)$ polynomial. One of its $n$ disk zeros is the factor zero at $z=0$; the remaining $n-1$ zeros are exactly those of the quotient. Dividing by the nonzero scalar $1-a_0^2$ changes no roots. Hence all zeros of $q$ lie strictly inside the disk.

before.claim: Each displayed block objective is the corresponding convex objective plus a nonnegative continuous quadratic in its block variable; the order fixes later blocks at their newest available values. The update is therefore precisely the sequential Gauss–Seidel extension of the two-block recurrence.

An exact update requires each argmin to be nonempty and attained. The definition requires explicit failure rather than an uncertified approximate point when a finite cap is exhausted, and makes no claim that the cap succeeds or that the outer sequence converges.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.

before.quote:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.
A saddle point means a saddle pair in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]].

For an exact outer sweep with scaled dual $u^k$, compute, in order,
$$x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_x\left(f(x)+\frac\rho2\|Kx+Lz^k-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
$$z^{k+1}\in\arg\min_z\left(g(z)+\frac\rho2\|Kx^{k+1}+Lz-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
then set $r^{k+1}=Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c$ and
$u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}$. Report also the unscaled dual
$y^k=\rho u^k$, objective $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$, and primal residual $r^k$.
If an exact subproblem has multiple minimizers, choose the unique minimum-norm
member of its nonempty closed convex minimizer set; existence and uniqueness of
that tie-break follow from [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]].

A finite implementation supplies finite inner iteration caps for both solves.
A solve is accepted only with a certificate of an attained global minimizer
before its cap. Return **invalid-input** for invalid dimensions or $\rho\le0$;
return **x-solve-failed**, **x-cap-exhausted**, **z-solve-failed**, or
**z-cap-exhausted** if the corresponding solve fails, is uncertified, or reaches
its cap. A failed sweep does not change the outer state, even if its first
subproblem was solved. These statuses give no approximate convergence guarantee.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and $\eta\ge0$, define
$$\partial_\eta g(x)=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(z)\ge g(x)+\langle p,z-x\rangle-\eta\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.$$
Write $\partial g(x)=\partial_0g(x)$. If $x\notin\operatorname{dom}g$, set $\partial_\eta g(x)=\varnothing$. When $g$ is finite-valued on a convex domain, $\partial g(x)$ agrees with [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]].

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

before.claim: Choose $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$ by [F3]. The affine minorant [F2] gives $\langle a,x\rangle-f(x)\le-b$ for every $x$ with finite $f(x)$, so $f^*(a)\le-b<+\infty$. The term at $x_0$ gives $f^*(a)\ge\langle a,x_0\rangle-f(x_0)>-\infty$. Thus $f^*$ is proper.

For each $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the map $s\mapsto\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)$ is finite continuous affine by [F4]. A pointwise supremum of these affine functions is convex: apply each affine function to $(1-\theta)s_0+\theta s_1$, bound by $(1-\theta)f^*(s_0)+\theta f^*(s_1)$, then take the supremum.

The epigraph of $f^*$ is the intersection, over $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, of the closed half-spaces $$\{(s,t):t\ge\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$ Each half-space is closed because its defining affine function is continuous, and any intersection of closed sets is closed. Hence $f^*$ is closed in the epigraph convention of [F3].

before.claim: If $f(x)=+\infty$, the left side is $+\infty$ because [F1] and properness ensure $f^*(s)>-\infty$, so the inequality is true and equality is impossible. If $f(x)<+\infty$, the term $z=x$ in [F1] gives $f^*(s)\ge\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)$, proving the inequality; if $f^*(s)=+\infty$, equality is again impossible.

Assume now $f(x)$ and $f^*(s)$ are finite. Equality in step 1.1 holds iff the supremum in [F1] equals its $z=x$ term, which is equivalent to $$\langle s,z\rangle-f(z)\le\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\quad\text{for every }z\in\operatorname{dom}f.$$ Rearranging gives precisely the inequalities in [F2]; for $z\notin\operatorname{dom}f$ they hold automatically. Thus equality is equivalent to $s\in\partial f(x)$, and the converse follows by reversing these inequalities.

after.claim: If $f(x)=+\infty$, the left side is $+\infty$ because [F1] and properness ensure $f^*(s)>-\infty$, so the inequality is true and equality is impossible. If $f(x)<+\infty$, the term $z=x$ in [F1] gives $f^*(s)\ge\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)$, proving the inequality; if $f^*(s)=+\infty$, equality is again impossible.

Assume now $f(x)$ and $f^*(s)$ are finite. Equality in step 1.1 holds iff the supremum in [F1] equals its $z=x$ term, which is equivalent to $$\langle s,z\rangle-f(z)\le\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\quad\text{for every }z\in\operatorname{dom}f.$$ Rearranging gives precisely the inequalities in [F2]; for $z\notin\operatorname{dom}f$ they hold automatically. Thus equality is equivalent to $s\in\partial f(x)$, and the converse follows by reversing these inequalities.

before.claim: Transform every graph pair $(x,a)\in A$ into $p=x+\rho a$ and $q=x-\rho a$. If two graph pairs are used, then $$\|q-q'\|_2^2\le\|p-p'\|_2^2,$$ because the difference of the right and left sides is $4\rho\langle x-x',a-a'\rangle\ge0$ by [F1]. Also, if $p=p'$, this inequality forces $q=q'$. Thus the rule $T(p)=q$ is a well-defined 1-Lipschitz map on its range $D=\{x+\rho a:(x,a)\in A\}$.

Fix arbitrary $y\in E$. By [F3], extend $T$ at $y$ by some $q$ satisfying $\|q-(x-\rho a)\|_2\le\|y-(x+\rho a)\|_2$ for every $(x,a)\in A$. Set $\tilde x=(y+q)/2$ and $\tilde a=(y-q)/(2\rho)$. Expanding the squared inequality shows $\langle\tilde x-x,\tilde a-a\rangle\ge0$ for every graph pair, so adjoining $(\tilde x,\tilde a)$ preserves monotonicity. By maximality in [F1], it already belongs to $A$. Hence $y=\tilde x+\rho\tilde a$, proving existence. This also covers an initially empty graph: [F3] gives the extension and maximality rules out the empty graph.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean

   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$

   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.

   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.

   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

before.claim: By [F1] and [F3], both proximal inputs in the recurrence are proper closed convex functions; [F2] supplies the defining conjugate expression for the dual term. If a proximal space has positive dimension, [F4] gives an everywhere unique output. Since $\tau,\sigma>0$, every exact update exists uniquely, including when $K=0$; the strict step inequality then reads $0<1$.

The three assignments fully specify the exact state and extrapolated value; $K^*$ in the primal update is the adjoint of [F6], and the step-size condition uses the induced norm [F5]. If either finite routine fails to certify its exact proximal output before its cap, the state is not advanced and the status is not a convergence certificate. before.quote:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its effective domain is $\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)<+\infty\}$. The function is **proper** if $\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing$; it is **convex** if
$$g((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le(1-\theta)g(x)+\theta g(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0\le\theta\le1),$$
using the endpoint convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functionals-on-a-banach-space]]. It is **closed** (equivalently, lower semicontinuous in the extended-real convex-analysis convention used here) if its epigraph
$$\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:g(x)\le s\}$$
is closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. The proximal-gradient items on this page assume $g$ is proper, closed and convex.

This page's closed-epigraph convention is explicit: it does not silently use an equivalence between sequential lower semicontinuity and topological closedness that would require an additional choice principle in the library's generic sequential convention. In finite dimensions this is the standard closed proper convex input to proximal algorithms.

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is the
extended-real function on the same Euclidean space
$$f^*(s):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$
When $f(x)=+\infty$, the corresponding term is $-\infty$ and does not increase
the supremum. Its effective domain is
$\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{s:f^*(s)<+\infty\}$.

If $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper, closed and convex, then its
conjugate $f^*$ from [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]]
is also proper, closed and convex. The affine-minorant result cited below is
used only to prove properness; closedness and convexity follow directly from
the supremum formula.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

before.claim: For every $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the right saddle inequality at $(x,z_*)$ and feasibility give $f(x)\ge f(x_*)+\langle-K^*y_*,x-x_*\rangle$; the same argument with $(x_*,z)$ gives $-L^*y_*\in\partial g(z_*)$. Thus [F4] gives both saddle subgradient inclusions. For $k\ge1$, the preceding exact sweep also gives $-L^*y^k\in\partial g(z^k)$ from [F2]. The inequalities at $z^{k+1}$ and $z^k$ read $g(z^{k+1})-g(z^k)\le-\langle y^{k+1},L\Delta z^{k+1}\rangle$ and $g(z^{k+1})-g(z^k)\ge-\langle y^k,L\Delta z^{k+1}\rangle$. Combining them gives $\langle y^{k+1}-y^k,L\Delta z^{k+1}\rangle\le0$. This is the sign needed below and is why the estimate starts at $k=1$.

Adding the two defining subgradient inequalities shows subgradient monotonicity. At the $f$-block this gives $0\le\langle a^{k+1}+K^*y_*,x^{k+1}-x_*\rangle=-\langle y^{k+1}-y_*,K(x^{k+1}-x_*)\rangle+\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},K(x^{k+1}-x_*)\rangle.$ At the $g$-block it gives $0\le\langle b^{k+1}+L^*y_*,z^{k+1}-z_*\rangle=-\langle y^{k+1}-y_*,L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle$. Add the two inequalities and use $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$ to obtain $\langle y^{k+1}-y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle\le\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},K(x^{k+1}-x_*)\rangle.$ Substitute $K(x^{k+1}-x_*)=r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)$.

The identity $y^{k+1}-y^k=\rho r^{k+1}$ gives $$\frac{\|y^{k+1}-y_*\|^2-\|y^k-y_*\|^2}{\rho} =2\langle y^{k+1}-y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle-\rho\|r^{k+1}\|^2.$$ The analogous expansion for $L(z^k-z_*)$ is $$\rho(\|L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\|^2-\|L(z^k-z_*)\|^2) =2\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle-\rho\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|^2.$$ Add these identities, use step 2.1, and then use step 1.1 to bound $2\langle y^{k+1}-y^k,L\Delta z^{k+1}\rangle\le0$. The asserted energy descent follows.

The two subgradient inequalities [F2,F4] at $(x^{k+1},z^{k+1})$ against $(x_*,z_*)$ give $p_{k+1}-p_*\le\langle a^{k+1},x^{k+1}-x_*\rangle+\langle b^{k+1},z^{k+1}-z_*\rangle=-\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},K(x^{k+1}-x_*)\rangle.$ Replace $K(x^{k+1}-x_*)$ by $r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)$ to obtain the upper estimate. The right saddle inequality [F3] at $(x^{k+1},z^{k+1})$ is $p_{k+1}+\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle\ge p_*$, which rearranges to the lower estimate.

before.claim: For any firmly nonexpansive $J$, its reflector $R=2J-I$ is nonexpansive: with $d=v-v'$ and $e=Jv-Jv'$, [F2] gives $$\|2e-d\|_2^2=\|d\|_2^2+4\|e\|_2^2-4\langle e,d\rangle\le\|d\|_2^2.$$ Thus $R_A R_B$ is nonexpansive because it is a composition of two nonexpansive maps.

Expanding the reflectors gives $T=(I+R_A R_B)/2$. For $d=w-w'$ and $s=R_AR_Bw-R_AR_Bw'$, nonexpansiveness gives $\|s\|_2\le\|d\|_2$, and $$\left\|\frac{d+s}{2}\right\|_2^2\le\left\langle\frac{d+s}{2},d\right\rangle$$ is equivalent after multiplying by $4$ and cancelling common terms to $\|s\|_2^2\le\|d\|_2^2$. This is the firm inequality for $T$.

before.quote:
Given maximal-monotone $A,B$ on $E=\mathbb R^n$, $\rho>0$, and $w_0\in E$,
define for $k\ge0$
$$p_k=J_{\rho B}(w_k),\qquad q_k=J_{\rho A}(2p_k-w_k),\qquad
w_{k+1}=w_k+q_k-p_k.$$
The **shadow** is $p_k$. Each exact update exists and is unique by
[[thm-maximal-monotone-resolvent-is-firmly-nonexpansive]]. This recurrence
specifies exact real arithmetic; a finite implementation that cannot evaluate
a resolvent must report failure and must not advance the exact recurrence. No
termination or convergence claim is part of this algorithm definition.

Let $A$ be maximal monotone on $E=\mathbb R^n$ and let $\rho>0$. For every
$y\in E$ there is a unique $x\in E$ with $y-x\in\rho A(x)$. Thus the
resolvent from [[def-resolvent-of-a-monotone-relation]] is an everywhere-defined
map and, for all $y,y'\in E$,
$$\|J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y'\|_2^2\le
\langle J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y',y-y'\rangle.$$
This is firm nonexpansiveness; it also implies the map is 1-Lipschitz.

before.claim: For each positive-dimensional proximal space, the optimality condition [F2] and extended-real subgradient definition [F3] give the relevant inequality. If a proximal space is zero-dimensional, [F6] says its only point is $0$; its update and test point are both $0$, so the same inequality is equality in that coordinate. Therefore in every dimension the two inequalities are $$g^*(y)-g^*(y^{k+1})\ge\left\langle\frac{y^k-y^{k+1}}\sigma+K\bar x^k,y-y^{k+1}\right\rangle,$$ $$f(x)-f(x^{k+1})\ge\left\langle\frac{x^k-x^{k+1}}\tau-K^*y^{k+1},x-x^{k+1}\right\rangle.$$ The identity $-\langle a-b,c-b\rangle=(\|c-a\|^2-\|c-b\|^2-\|b-a\|^2)/2$ applied to the primal and dual displacement terms gives the two distance differences $E_k-E_{k+1}-X_{k+1}$ and $E_k-E_{k+1}-Y_{k+1}$ in their respective coordinates. The bilinear terms from the primal inequality and the gap expand as $\langle y^{k+1},K(x-x^{k+1})\rangle+\langle Kx^{k+1},y\rangle-\langle Kx,y^{k+1}\rangle=\langle Kx^{k+1},y-y^{k+1}\rangle$. Adding the dual update term $\langle K\bar x^k,y^{k+1}-y\rangle$ gives $\langle K(\bar x^k-x^{k+1}),y^{k+1}-y\rangle$ in the upper bound for $G_{k+1}$. Moving this term to the other side yields $$E_k\ge G_{k+1}+E_{k+1}+X_{k+1}+Y_{k+1}+\langle K(x^{k+1}-\bar x^k),y^{k+1}-y\rangle,$$ where $G_{k+1}=\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})$, $E_j=\|x-x^j\|^2/(2\tau)+\|y-y^j\|^2/(2\sigma)$, $X_j=\|x^j-x^{j-1}\|^2/(2\tau)$, and $Y_j=\|y^j-y^{j-1}\|^2/(2\sigma)$.

Define $x^{-1}=x^0$, so $X_0=0$, and $B_k=\langle K(x^k-x^{k-1}),y^k-y\rangle$. The extrapolation in [F1] gives $$\langle K(x^{k+1}-\bar x^k),y^{k+1}-y\rangle =B_{k+1}-B_k-\langle K(x^k-x^{k-1}),y^{k+1}-y^k\rangle.$$ By [F4,F5] and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$, $$|\langle K(x^k-x^{k-1}),y^{k+1}-y^k\rangle| \le\kappa(X_k+Y_{k+1}).$$ Substitution into step 1.1 therefore gives $$E_k\ge G_{k+1}+E_{k+1}+(1-\kappa)Y_{k+1}+X_{k+1}-\kappa X_k+B_{k+1}-B_k.$$

Sum step 2.1 for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$. The $B$ terms telescope, $B_0=0$, and the $X$ terms satisfy $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(X_{k+1}-\kappa X_k)=(1-\kappa)\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}X_k+X_N\ge0$. Thus $$\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}G_{k+1}+E_N+(1-\kappa)\sum_{k=1}^N Y_k +(1-\kappa)\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}X_k+X_N+B_N\le E_0.$$ For the terminal cross term, [F4,F5] and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ give $$-B_N\le\|K\|_2\|x^N-x^{N-1}\|_2\|y^N-y\|_2 \le X_N+\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2\frac{\|y^N-y\|_2^2}{2\sigma}.$$ Since $E_N$ contains $\|y^N-y\|^2/(2\sigma)$ and $\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2=\kappa^2<1$, these terminal terms leave a nonnegative remainder; all increment terms are also nonnegative because $\kappa<1$. Drop them to obtain $\sum G_{k+1}\le E_0$, the claimed estimate. When $K=0$, $\kappa=0$ and the same inequalities hold without division by $\|K\|_2$.

before.quote:
Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$, let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, and let $K:X\to Y$ be
linear. Its unique adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$ exists by
[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]], including zero-dimensional
spaces. Identify $K$ with its matrix in the standard Euclidean bases when using
the induced matrix norm below. The primal problem is $\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)$, with saddle function
$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$
where $g^*$ is defined by [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]].
The saddle function $\Phi$ is evaluated on
$\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g^*$, where both function values
are finite; no undefined extended-real subtraction is used outside this domain.
Assume $\tau,\sigma>0$ and
$\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2<1$, where $\|K\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator
norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Starting from $x^0,y^0$ and
$\bar x^0=x^0$, the exact recurrence is
$$y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
In positive-dimensional spaces the proximal maps are everywhere single-valued
by [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; in a
zero-dimensional space its sole input and output are the zero vector, so that
proximal call is single-valued directly. The proper closed convexity of $g^*$
follows from [[lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-convex]]. A finite implementation
uses finite call caps and advances an iterate only after both exact proximal
outputs are certified; otherwise it returns **prox-call-failed** or
**prox-cap-exhausted** and makes no convergence claim for that run.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.

Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and $\eta\ge0$, define

([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$

the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,

formulas above are not asserted in this case.

inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];

[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.

   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

before.claim: The left saddle inequality forces $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$: otherwise taking $y=y_*+t(Kx_*+Lz_*-c)$ and letting $t\to+\infty$ contradicts its finite upper bound. The right saddle inequality then says every feasible pair has objective at least $p_*$, so $(x_*,z_*)$ is primal optimal. For every $y$, the dual value $d(y)$ is at most $\mathcal L((x_*,z_*),y)=p_*$. At $y_*$, the right saddle inequality gives $d(y_*)\ge p_*$; hence $d(y_*)=p_*$ and $y_*$ is dual optimal.

Fixing $z=z_*$ and then $x=x_*$ in the right saddle inequality gives $-K^*y_*\in\partial f(x_*)$ and $-L^*y_*\in\partial g(z_*)$. By [F6], $f(x_*)+f^*(-K^*y_*)=-\langle y_*,Kx_*\rangle,\qquad g(z_*)+g^*(-L^*y_*)=-\langle y_*,Lz_*\rangle.$ Each component infimum is below a finite value because $f,g$ are proper, so neither equals $+\infty$. If both are finite, choosing independent points within any $\epsilon>0$ of them proves that the joint infimum is their sum; if either is $-\infty$, fixing a finite competitor in the other block and sending the first block value down shows the joint infimum is $-\infty$. Thus separating the $x$ and $z$ infima and using [F4] gives the extended-real identity $$d(y)=-f^*(-K^*y)-g^*(-L^*y)-\langle y,c\rangle.$$ The terms are well-defined because [F5] excludes $-\infty$ conjugate values. Substituting the two equalities and feasibility into the formula gives $d(y_*)=p_*$. The dual solution set $Y_*:=\{y:d(y)=p_*\}$ is nonempty. Weak duality gives $d(y)\le p_*$, so $y\in Y_*$ iff $\mathcal L((x,z),y)\ge p_*$ for every $x,z$. Each finite-valued pair $(x,z)$ imposes a closed affine half-space in $y$; an infinite-valued pair imposes no restriction. Thus $Y_*$ is closed and convex as an intersection of closed convex sets.

Sum the descent inequality [F3] from $k=1$ to $N$. Since $V^{N+1}\ge0$, $$\sum_{k=1}^N\bigl(\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2+\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2\bigr)\le V^1/\rho.$$ Each nonnegative term of a convergent bounded partial sum tends to zero, so $r^k\to0$ and $L\Delta z^k\to0$. The energy bound also makes $y^k$ and $L(z^k-z_*)$ bounded.

The objective estimates [F3] now force convergence. In the upper estimate, $\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle\to0$ by boundedness and residual convergence; both terms paired with $L\Delta z^{k+1}$ tend to zero because $r^{k+1}\to0$ and $L(z^{k+1}-z_*)$ is bounded. The lower estimate $p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle$ also tends to zero. Hence $p_{k+1}\to p_*$.

The subgradient inequalities underlying [F3] imply, for every fixed $x,z$ and every sweep, $$f(x)+g(z)+\langle y^{k+1},Kx+Lz-c\rangle\ge p_{k+1}+\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},Kx-Kx^{k+1}\rangle.$$ Indeed, apply the $f$- and $g$-subgradient inclusions [F8] at the new iterates, use their defining inequalities, add them, and substitute $Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c=r^{k+1}$.

Along any convergent subsequence $y^{k_j+1}\to\bar y$, the quantities $Kx^{k_j+1}=c-Lz^{k_j+1}+r^{k_j+1}$ are bounded by step 2.2. Taking limits in step 1.2, using steps 2.2–2.2, gives $$f(x)+g(z)+\langle\bar y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle\ge p_*\qquad\text{for all }x,z.$$ Since the primal optimizer is feasible, $d(\bar y)\ge p_*$, while weak duality from step 1.1 gives $d(\bar y)\le p_*$. Thus every dual cluster point belongs to $Y_*$. The inequality at the fixed primal optimizer also makes it a saddle point with $\bar y$.

If $p=0$, then $\mathbb R^p=\{0\}$ by [F10], so $y^k=0$ for every $k$; step 2.1 shows this unique dual vector is optimal, and dual convergence follows. Assume henceforth $p\ge1$. Boundedness from step 2.2 and [F7] give at least one dual cluster point. Let $y_1,y_2\in Y_*$ be any two cluster points. Each pairs with the same primal optimizer to form a saddle point, so [F3] makes both energy sequences $$V^k(y_i)=\rho^{-1}\|y^k-y_i\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2\quad(i=1,2)$$ nonincreasing from $k=1$ and bounded below; each therefore converges. Expanding the two squared norms gives $V^k(y_1)-V^k(y_2)=\frac2\rho\langle y^k,y_2-y_1\rangle+\frac{\|y_1\|_2^2-\|y_2\|_2^2}{\rho},$ so $\langle y^k,y_2-y_1\rangle$ converges. Along subsequences tending to $y_1$ and $y_2$ the limits are equal, so $\langle y_1-y_2,y_2-y_1\rangle=-\|y_1-y_2\|_2^2=0$ and $y_1=y_2$.

In the remaining case $p\ge1$, there is exactly one cluster point. If the bounded sequence $y^k$ did not converge to it, some subsequence would stay a fixed positive distance away; [F7] would give a convergent subsubsequence with a different cluster point, a contradiction. Therefore the whole unscaled dual sequence converges to a point of $Y_*$. No convergence of primal iterates was used.
