Substituting the two equalities and feasibility into the formula gives $d(y_*)=p_*$. The dual solution set $Y_*:=\{y:d(y)=p_*\}$ is nonempty. Weak duality gives $d(y)\le p_*$, so $y\in Y_*$ iff $\mathcal L((x,z),y)\ge p_*$ for every $x,z$. Each finite-valued pair $(x,z)$ imposes a closed affine half-space in $y$; an infinite-valued pair imposes no restriction. Thus $Y_*$ is closed and convex as an intersection of closed convex sets.

Sum the descent inequality [F3] from $k=1$ to $N$. Since $V^{N+1}\ge0$, $$\sum_{k=1}^N\bigl(\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2+\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2\bigr)\le V^1/\rho.$$ Each nonnegative term of a convergent bounded partial sum tends to zero, so $r^k\to0$ and $L\Delta z^k\to0$. The energy bound also makes $y^k$ and $L(z^k-z_*)$ bounded.

The objective estimates [F3] now force convergence. In the upper estimate, $\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle\to0$ by boundedness and residual convergence; both terms paired with $L\Delta z^{k+1}$ tend to zero because $r^{k+1}\to0$ and $L(z^{k+1}-z_*)$ is bounded. The lower estimate $p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle$ also tends to zero. Hence $p_{k+1}\to p_*$.

Along any convergent subsequence $y^{k_j+1}\to\bar y$, the quantities $Kx^{k_j+1}=c-Lz^{k_j+1}+r^{k_j+1}$ are bounded by step 2.2. Taking limits in step 1.2, using steps 2.2–2.2, gives $$f(x)+g(z)+\langle\bar y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle\ge p_*\qquad\text{for all }x,z.$$ Since the primal optimizer is feasible, $d(\bar y)\ge p_*$, while weak duality from step 1.1 gives $d(\bar y)\le p_*$. Thus every dual cluster point belongs to $Y_*$. The inequality at the fixed primal optimizer also makes it a saddle point with $\bar y$.

If $p=0$, then $\mathbb R^p=\{0\}$ by [F10], so $y^k=0$ for every $k$; step 2.1 shows this unique dual vector is optimal, and dual convergence follows. Assume henceforth $p\ge1$. Boundedness from step 2.2 and [F7] give at least one dual cluster point. Let $y_1,y_2\in Y_*$ be any two cluster points. Each pairs with the same primal optimizer to form a saddle point, so [F3] makes both energy sequences $$V^k(y_i)=\rho^{-1}\|y^k-y_i\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2\quad(i=1,2)$$ nonincreasing from $k=1$ and bounded below; each therefore converges. Expanding the two squared norms gives $V^k(y_1)-V^k(y_2)=\frac2\rho\langle y^k,y_2-y_1\rangle+\frac{\|y_1\|_2^2-\|y_2\|_2^2}{\rho},$ so $\langle y^k,y_2-y_1\rangle$ converges. Along subsequences tending to $y_1$ and $y_2$ the limits are equal, so $\langle y_1-y_2,y_2-y_1\rangle=-\|y_1-y_2\|_2^2=0$ and $y_1=y_2$.

In the remaining case $p\ge1$, there is exactly one cluster point. If the bounded sequence $y^k$ did not converge to it, some subsequence would stay a fixed positive distance away; [F7] would give a convergent subsubsequence with a different cluster point, a contradiction. Therefore the whole unscaled dual sequence converges to a point of $Y_*$. No convergence of primal iterates was used.

before.quote:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.
A saddle point means a saddle pair in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]].

For an exact outer sweep with scaled dual $u^k$, compute, in order,
$$x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_x\left(f(x)+\frac\rho2\|Kx+Lz^k-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
$$z^{k+1}\in\arg\min_z\left(g(z)+\frac\rho2\|Kx^{k+1}+Lz-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
then set $r^{k+1}=Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c$ and
$u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}$. Report also the unscaled dual
$y^k=\rho u^k$, objective $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$, and primal residual $r^k$.
If an exact subproblem has multiple minimizers, choose the unique minimum-norm
member of its nonempty closed convex minimizer set; existence and uniqueness of
that tie-break follow from [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]].

A finite implementation supplies finite inner iteration caps for both solves.
A solve is accepted only with a certificate of an attained global minimizer
before its cap. Return **invalid-input** for invalid dimensions or $\rho\le0$;
return **x-solve-failed**, **x-cap-exhausted**, **z-solve-failed**, or
**z-cap-exhausted** if the corresponding solve fails, is uncertified, or reaches
its cap. A failed sweep does not change the outer state, even if its first
subproblem was solved. These statuses give no approximate convergence guarantee.

Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

Suppose proper closed convex $f,g$ have a saddle point $(x_*,z_*,y_*)$ for the
Lagrangian in [[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]], with $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$, and every
subproblem in the exact ADMM sequence is attained. Put
$\Delta z^{k+1}=z^{k+1}-z^k$ and
$$V^k=\frac1\rho\|y^k-y_*\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2.$$
For every $k\ge1$,
$$V^{k+1}\le V^k-\rho\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2-\rho\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2.$$
The index begins at $k=1$: an arbitrary initial $z^0$ need not satisfy a
previous $z$-subproblem optimality condition. Also, with $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$
and $p_*=f(x_*)+g(z_*)$, every exact sweep satisfies
$$p_{k+1}-p_*\le-\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+
\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle,$$
$$p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle.$$

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is the
extended-real function on the same Euclidean space
$$f^*(s):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$
When $f(x)=+\infty$, the corresponding term is $-\infty$ and does not increase
the supremum. Its effective domain is
$\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{s:f^*(s)<+\infty\}$.

If $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper, closed and convex, then its
conjugate $f^*$ from [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]]
is also proper, closed and convex. The affine-minorant result cited below is
used only to prove properness; closedness and convexity follow directly from
the supremum formula.

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex. For every
$x,s\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)+f^*(s)\ge\langle s,x\rangle,$$
with extended-real interpretation. Equality holds exactly when
$x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $f^*(s)<+\infty$, and
$s\in\partial f(x)$; equivalently, for proper convex $f$, equality itself
forces the two finiteness conditions and the subgradient membership.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

For any exact two-block ADMM sweep from
[[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]], put
$\Delta z^{k+1}=z^{k+1}-z^k$ and $y^{k+1}=\rho u^{k+1}$. Then
$$-K^*(y^{k+1}-\rho L\Delta z^{k+1})\in\partial f(x^{k+1}),\qquad -L^*y^{k+1}\in\partial g(z^{k+1}).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of

[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

before.claim: Choose $b\in B(p)$ and $a\in A(p)$ with $a+b=0$. The resolvent identities give $J_{\rho B}(p+\rho b)=p$ and $J_{\rho A}(p-\rho b)=p$. At $w_*=p+\rho b$, the second input is $2p-w_*=p-\rho b$, so the update has $p_B=q=p$ and $T(w_*)=w_*$. Thus $T$ has a fixed point.
Apply [F3] using firm nonexpansiveness [F2]. It follows that the states $w_k=T^k(w_0)$ converge to some $w_*'$ with $T(w_*')=w_*'$.
Put $p'=J_{\rho B}(w_*')$ and $q'=J_{\rho A}(2p'-w_*')$. Fixedness says $q'=p'$. The resolvent inclusions yield $w_*'-p'\in\rho B(p')$ and $p'-w_*'\in\rho A(p')$; adding them gives $0\in(A+B)(p')$.
The shadow $p_k=J_{\rho B}(w_k)$ converges to $p'$ because the resolvent is 1-Lipschitz by [F4] and $w_k\to w_*'$. Thus the shadow converges to a zero of the sum.

before.quote:
Given maximal-monotone $A,B$ on $E=\mathbb R^n$, $\rho>0$, and $w_0\in E$,
define for $k\ge0$
$$p_k=J_{\rho B}(w_k),\qquad q_k=J_{\rho A}(2p_k-w_k),\qquad
w_{k+1}=w_k+q_k-p_k.$$
The **shadow** is $p_k$. Each exact update exists and is unique by
[[thm-maximal-monotone-resolvent-is-firmly-nonexpansive]]. This recurrence
specifies exact real arithmetic; a finite implementation that cannot evaluate
a resolvent must report failure and must not advance the exact recurrence. No
termination or convergence claim is part of this algorithm definition.

For maximal-monotone $A,B$ and $\rho>0$, let
$$T=I-J_{\rho B}+J_{\rho A}(2J_{\rho B}-I).$$
Then $T:E\to E$ is firmly nonexpansive:
$$\|T(w)-T(w')\|_2^2\le\langle T(w)-T(w'),w-w'\rangle.$$

Let $T:E\to E$ be firmly nonexpansive on $E=\mathbb R^n$, suppose
$\operatorname{Fix}(T)=\{p:T(p)=p\}$ is nonempty, and start at any $w_0$.
Then the Picard sequence $w_{k+1}=T(w_k)$ converges to a fixed point of $T$.

Let $A$ be maximal monotone on $E=\mathbb R^n$ and let $\rho>0$. For every
$y\in E$ there is a unique $x\in E$ with $y-x\in\rho A(x)$. Thus the
resolvent from [[def-resolvent-of-a-monotone-relation]] is an everywhere-defined

\langle J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y',y-y'\rangle.$$
This is firm nonexpansiveness; it also implies the map is 1-Lipschitz.

before.claim: Every exact proximal output lies in the effective domain of its function. Convexity therefore puts $\bar x_N$ in $\operatorname{dom}f$ and $\bar y_N$ in $\operatorname{dom}g^*$.

By convexity in [F1], $f(\bar x_N)\le N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}f(x^{k+1})$ and $g^*(\bar y_N)\le N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}g^*(y^{k+1})$; linearity gives $K\bar x_N=N^{-1}\sum Kx^{k+1}$. Hence $$\Phi(\bar x_N,y)-\Phi(x,\bar y_N) \le\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})\bigr).$$ Apply [F2] and divide by $N$ to get the bound.

By the saddle inequalities [F3], $\Phi(\bar x_N,y_*)\ge\Phi(x_*,y_*)$ and $\Phi(x_*,\bar y_N)\le\Phi(x_*,y_*)$, so their difference is nonnegative. Step 2.1 at $(x_*,y_*)$ supplies the same $O(1/N)$ upper bound. The ergodic estimate makes no claim about a single nonaveraged objective difference or pointwise iterate convergence.

before.quote:
Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$, let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, and let $K:X\to Y$ be
linear. Its unique adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$ exists by
[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]], including zero-dimensional
spaces. Identify $K$ with its matrix in the standard Euclidean bases when using
the induced matrix norm below. The primal problem is $\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)$, with saddle function
$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$
where $g^*$ is defined by [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]].
The saddle function $\Phi$ is evaluated on
$\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g^*$, where both function values
are finite; no undefined extended-real subtraction is used outside this domain.
Assume $\tau,\sigma>0$ and
$\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2<1$, where $\|K\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator
norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Starting from $x^0,y^0$ and
$\bar x^0=x^0$, the exact recurrence is
$$y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
In positive-dimensional spaces the proximal maps are everywhere single-valued
by [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; in a
zero-dimensional space its sole input and output are the zero vector, so that
proximal call is single-valued directly. The proper closed convexity of $g^*$
follows from [[lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-convex]]. A finite implementation
uses finite call caps and advances an iterate only after both exact proximal
outputs are certified; otherwise it returns **prox-call-failed** or
**prox-cap-exhausted** and makes no convergence claim for that run.

For the exact recurrence of [[alg-pdhg-primal-dual-hybrid-gradient]], put
$\kappa=\sqrt{\tau\sigma}\,\|K\|_2<1$ and
$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)$. For every
$x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $y\in\operatorname{dom}g^*$ and integer $N\ge1$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})\bigr)
\le\frac{\|x-x^0\|_2^2}{2\tau}+\frac{\|y-y^0\|_2^2}{2\sigma}.$$
The formula includes $K=0$ and uses $\bar x^0=x^0$.

Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

before.claim: Write the columns of $A$ as $a_1=(1,1,1)^T$, $a_2=(1,1,2)^T$, $a_3=(1,2,2)^T$. Their squared norms are $3,6,9$, so every scalar block subproblem has a strictly positive quadratic coefficient and a unique attained minimizer. Also $det A=-1$, so $Ax=0$ has only $x=0$. The dual function is $d(y)=inf_x\langle y,Ax\rangle$: it is $0$ when $A^Ty=0$ and $-\infty$ otherwise. Since $A$ is invertible, $A^Ty=0$ only for $y=0$, so the dual optimum is unique.

For state $s^k=(x_2^k,x_3^k,u_1^k,u_2^k,u_3^k)^T$, exact differentiation of the three scalar subproblems gives $x_1^{k+1}=-\frac{a_1^T(u^k+a_2x_2^k+a_3x_3^k)}3$, $x_2^{k+1}=-\frac{a_2^T(u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_3x_3^k)}6$, and $x_3^{k+1}=-\frac{a_3^T(u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_2x_2^{k+1})}9$. Substitute these into $u^{k+1}=u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_2x_2^{k+1}+a_3x_3^{k+1}$; exact rational simplification gives $s^{k+1}=Ms^k$ with $$M=\frac1{162}\begin{pmatrix}144&-9&9&9&-18\\8&157&5&-13&8\\-64&-122&122&-58&-64\\-56&35&-35&91&-56\\88&26&-26&-62&88\end{pmatrix}.$$ The vector $v=(0,0,1,1,1)^T$ satisfies $Mv=0$. Exact rational matrix multiplication gives $p_1=\operatorname{tr}(M)=\frac{301}{81}$, $p_2=\operatorname{tr}(M^2)=\frac{20860}{6561}$, $p_3=\operatorname{tr}(M^3)=\frac{2588159}{1062882}$, and $p_4=\operatorname{tr}(M^4)=\frac{132553799}{86093442}$. Newton's identities $e_1=p_1$, $e_2=(p_1^2-p_2)/2$, $e_3=(p_3-e_1p_2+e_2p_1)/3$, and $e_4=(-p_4+e_1p_3-e_2p_2+e_3p_1)/4$ give $e_1=301/81$, $e_2=287/54$, $e_3=280/81$, $e_4=70/81$; $Mv=0$ gives $e_5=\det M=0$. Therefore $\det(\lambda I-M)=\lambda q(\lambda)$, where $q(\lambda)=\lambda^4-\frac{301}{81}\lambda^3+\frac{287}{54}\lambda^2-\frac{280}{81}\lambda+\frac{70}{81}$.

For $z=e^{it}$, direct expansion gives $\operatorname{Im}(e^{-2it}q(e^{it}))=\frac{\sin t(22\cos t-21)}{81}$. If this vanishes because $\sin t=0$, substitution gives $q(1)=1/162$ and $q(-1)=775/54$, both nonzero. Otherwise $\cos t=21/22$, and substitution into the real part gives $\operatorname{Re}(e^{-2it}q(e^{it}))=19/19602\ne0$. Thus $q$ has no unit-circle zero.

Suppose every zero of $q$ lies inside the unit disk. By [F2], its normalized Schur reduction is the stable monic cubic $q_1(z)=z^3-\frac{4781}{1661}z^2+\frac{861}{302}z-\frac{1610}{1661}$. Since $|q_1(0)|=1610/1661<1$, another application gives the stable monic quadratic $q_2(z)=z^2-\frac{317086}{166821}z+\frac{336511}{333642}$. By [F3], $q_2$ factors as $(z-\zeta_1)(z-\zeta_2)$ over $\mathbb C$, with both roots inside the unit disk by the reductions. Its constant term is $\zeta_1\zeta_2$, so $|q_2(0)|=|\zeta_1||\zeta_2|<1$, contradicting $q_2(0)=336511/333642>1$. Therefore not all zeros of $q$ lie inside. The coefficients of $q_1,q_2$ follow by substituting into $(p-p(0)p^\#)/(z(1-p(0)^2))$ and collecting powers.

By [F3], $q$ has four roots counted with multiplicity. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 show that none is on the unit circle and not all are inside, so some root $\lambda$ satisfies $|\lambda|>1$. Since $\det(\lambda I-M)=\lambda q(\lambda)=0$ by step 1.2, [F4] gives a nonzero complex vector $v$ with $Mv=\lambda v$. Suppose each of the five standard basis vectors $e_j\in\mathbb Q^5$ had a bounded orbit under $M$. Then every column of $M^k$ would be uniformly bounded in $k$, and since there are only five columns, every entry would be bounded by one common constant $C$. Choose $i$ with $v_i\ne0$. The finite-sum triangle inequality would give $|(M^kv)_i|\le C\sum_j|v_j|$ for every $k$, but $M^kv=\lambda^kv$ makes $|(M^kv)_i|=|\lambda|^k|v_i|\to\infty$, a contradiction. Hence at least one standard basis vector has an unbounded orbit. Taking $s^0=e_j$ for that index and $x_1^0=0$ gives a rational initial state with unbounded iterates; each subproblem remains uniquely attained as shown in step 1.1.

before.claim: On the feasible set $z=x$, the objective is $$f(x)+g(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2+\tfrac12(x+1)^2=x^2+1,$$ which is uniquely minimized at $x=z=0$ with value $1$. For $y_*=1$, $$\mathcal L((x,z),1)=f(x)+g(z)+x-z=1+\tfrac12x^2+\tfrac12z^2\ge1,$$ with equality at $(0,0)$; feasibility makes $\mathcal L((0,0),y)=1$ for every $y$. These are exactly the saddle inequalities [F2].

The equality matrix is $A=(1,-1)$, whose single row is linearly independent, so the dual definition [F3] applies. Its dual function is $$d(y)=\inf_x\{\tfrac12(x-1)^2+yx\}+\inf_z\{\tfrac12(z+1)^2-yz\}=(y-\tfrac12y^2)+(y-\tfrac12y^2)=1-(y-1)^2.$$ Thus its maximum is $1$ at $y=1$, consistent with weak duality [F4] and the saddle value.

Differentiating the first strictly convex quadratic in [F1] gives $2x^{k+1}=1+z^k-u^k$. At $k=0$ this yields $x^1=1/2$. Differentiating the second gives $2z^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+u^k-1$, hence $z^1=-1/4$ and then $u^1=u^0+x^1-z^1=3/4$.

The same two equations give $x^2=(1-1/4-3/4)/2=0$, $z^2=(0+3/4-1)/2=-1/8$, and $u^2=3/4+0-(-1/8)=7/8$. Each subproblem is a strictly convex quadratic, so both minimizers in each of these sweeps are attained and unique. The recurrence values are exact rationals.

Let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and let $b$ be a
vector of matching size. Define

$$K_0(A,b):=\{0\},$$

and for $m\ge 1$ define the $m$th **Krylov subspace**

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with ordered eigenvalues
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n$. Let $r$ be the multiplicity of $\lambda_1$.
If $r<n$, assume $\lambda_1>\lambda_{r+1}$, and let $P$ be the orthogonal
projection onto the $\lambda_1$-eigenspace. Let $b\in\mathbb R^n$ be a unit
vector and, for $m\ge1$, define

$$K_m:=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\ldots,A^{m-1}b\},\qquad \theta_m:=\max_{0\ne x\in K_m}\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}x}.$$

Thus $\theta_m$ is the largest Rayleigh–Ritz value on $K_m$; if Lanczos runs
through step $m$ without breakdown, it is the largest Ritz value of
$Q_m^{\mathsf T}AQ_m$. If $r=n$, then $A=\lambda_1I$ and $\theta_m=\lambda_1$
for every $m\ge1$. Suppose $r<n$.

1. If $Pb=0$, then $\theta_m\le\lambda_{r+1}$ for every $m$; no convergence
   to $\lambda_1$ is asserted.

2. If $Pb\ne0$, put
   $$\tau:=\frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2}{\|Pb\|_2}.$$
   If $\lambda_{r+1}>\lambda_n$, then for every $m\ge1$,
   $$0\le\lambda_1-\theta_m\le \frac{(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\tau^2} {T_{m-1}\!\left(1+2\frac{\lambda_1-\lambda_{r+1}} {\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_n}\right)^2}.$$
   For a simple top eigenvalue ($r=1$), $\tau$ is the tangent of the angle
   between $b$ and a unit top eigenvector, so the starting-angle denominator
   is explicit.

3. If $\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_n$, then
   $$\lambda_1-\theta_1=(\lambda_1-\lambda_n) \frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2^2}{\|b\|_2^2},\qquad \theta_m=\lambda_1\quad(m\ge2).$$

When $r<n$, $Pb\ne0$, and exact Lanczos breakdown occurs at dimension $d$, then
$\theta_d=\lambda_1$ and $K_m=K_d$ for all $m\ge d$. These are exact-arithmetic
claims; they give no finite-precision grade-termination guarantee.

Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$, let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, and let $K:X\to Y$ be
linear. Its unique adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$ exists by
[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]], including zero-dimensional
spaces. Identify $K$ with its matrix in the standard Euclidean bases when using
the induced matrix norm below. The primal problem is $\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)$, with saddle function
$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$
where $g^*$ is defined by [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]].
The saddle function $\Phi$ is evaluated on
$\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g^*$, where both function values
are finite; no undefined extended-real subtraction is used outside this domain.
Assume $\tau,\sigma>0$ and
$\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2<1$, where $\|K\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator
norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Starting from $x^0,y^0$ and
$\bar x^0=x^0$, the exact recurrence is
$$y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
In positive-dimensional spaces the proximal maps are everywhere single-valued
by [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; in a
zero-dimensional space its sole input and output are the zero vector, so that
proximal call is single-valued directly. The proper closed convexity of $g^*$
follows from [[lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-convex]]. A finite implementation
uses finite call caps and advances an iterate only after both exact proximal
outputs are certified; otherwise it returns **prox-call-failed** or
**prox-cap-exhausted** and makes no convergence claim for that run.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

before.claim: The record has valid row pointers $0=r_0\le r_1=2=s$ and valid columns $0,1$. By [F2,F3], its exact matrix-vector product is $-x_0+x_1$; its transpose sends $y$ to $(-y,y)$. By [F4], its stored-entry count is $s=2$, slot count is $6$, and the exact operation count is two multiplications, two additions, and one output initialization.

The conjugate of $g(v)=|v|$ is the indicator of $[-1,1]$: if $|y|\le1$, then $yv-|v|\le0$ for every $v$ and equality occurs at $v=0$; if $y>1$, taking $v\to+\infty$ makes the supremum infinite, and if $y<-1$, taking $v\to-\infty$ does so. Initially $K\bar x^0=0$, so $y^1=\operatorname{proj}_{[-1,1]}(0)=0$, then $x^1=(0+(1/2)(1,0))/(3/2)=(1/3,0)$. Thus $\bar x^1=(2/3,0)$ and $y^2=\operatorname{proj}_{[-1,1]}((1/2)K\bar x^1) =\operatorname{proj}_{[-1,1]}(-1/3)=-1/3$.

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

Fix a field $F$. The **validated CSR matrix-vector product** takes integer
dimension candidates $m,n$, integer arrays $r,c$, a value array $v$ of elements
of $F$, and a vector candidate $x$ of elements of $F$. All input arrays are
finite; write $s=\operatorname{length}(v)$.

1. If $m\notin\mathbb N$, $n\notin\mathbb N$,
   $\operatorname{length}(r)\ne m+1$,
   $\operatorname{length}(c)\ne s$, or
   $\operatorname{length}(x)\ne n$, return the status `invalid-dimension`.
2. For $i=0,\ldots,m$, check that $r_i\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$; return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails. Check $r_0=0$ and $r_m=s$, and for each
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$ check $r_i\le r_{i+1}$; return `invalid-index` if any
   check fails. For each $t=0,\ldots,s-1$, check $0\le c_t<n$ and return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails.
3. Initialize $y_i=0_F$ for $0\le i<m$. For each row
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$, and then each stored index
   $t=r_i,\ldots,r_{i+1}-1$, update
   $$y_i\gets y_i+v_t x_{c_t}.$$
4. Return the status `ok` together with $y\in F^m$.

For valid CSR data this uses exact field operations. Validation examines only
finite arrays, and the row intervals partition the $s$ stored entries, so the
specified loops are bounded. This procedure makes no floating-point rounding,
backward-stability, convergence, runtime, or memory-bandwidth claim.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let a valid CSR record represent
$A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, and let $x=(x_j)_{j<n}\in F^n$. Define
$(Ax)_i:=\sum_{j<n}A_{ij}x_j$, the usual matrix-vector product from
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Then the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] returns `ok` with output
$Ax$ in exact field arithmetic.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, and let a valid CSR record have
$s$ stored entries. Its input arrays use exactly $s$ field-value slots, $s$
integer column-index slots, and $m+1$ integer row-pointer slots, for a total of
$2s+m+1$ data slots. On valid input, the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] performs exactly $s$ field
multiplications, $s$ field additions, and $m$ zero initializations. Its index
validation and loop-control work is $O(m+s+1)$. Counting the CSR arrays and
returned output but excluding the supplied vector $x$ and constant-size
workspace, it uses exactly $2s+2m+1$ data slots, hence $O(m+s+1)$ slots; for
$m\ge1$ this is $O(m+s)$. Here $O(g)$ means bounded by $Cg$ for a constant $C$ independent of
the dimensions and input values.

For a square record of order $m\ge1$ with at least one stored entry in each
row, $s\ge m$, so the work and storage are $O(s)$. For a canonical record as defined in
[[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]], $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$;
without that convention, the cost is in terms of stored entries, not
$\operatorname{nnz}(A)$. These are arithmetic, index, and storage counts, not

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Assume the hypotheses of [[alg-pdhg-primal-dual-hybrid-gradient]] and that
$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)$ has a saddle point
$(x_*,y_*)$ in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]]. For $N\ge1$ define
$$\bar x_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x^{k+1},\qquad
\bar y_N=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}y^{k+1}.$$
For every $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $y\in\operatorname{dom}g^*$,
$$\Phi(\bar x_N,y)-\Phi(x,\bar y_N)
\le\frac1N\left(\frac{\|x-x^0\|_2^2}{2\tau}
+\frac{\|y-y^0\|_2^2}{2\sigma}\right).$$
In particular, the saddle gap
$\Phi(\bar x_N,y_*)-\Phi(x_*,\bar y_N)$ is nonnegative and obeys this bound
with $(x,y)=(x_*,y_*)$. On bounded test sets the displayed upper bound is
$O(1/N)$. This is an ergodic gap statement; it is not a pointwise objective
bound and does not assert pointwise iterate convergence.

Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$, let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, and let $K:X\to Y$ be
linear. Its unique adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$ exists by
[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]], including zero-dimensional
spaces. Identify $K$ with its matrix in the standard Euclidean bases when using
the induced matrix norm below. The primal problem is $\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)$, with saddle function
$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$
where $g^*$ is defined by [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]].
The saddle function $\Phi$ is evaluated on
$\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g^*$, where both function values
are finite; no undefined extended-real subtraction is used outside this domain.
Assume $\tau,\sigma>0$ and
$\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2<1$, where $\|K\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator
norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Starting from $x^0,y^0$ and
$\bar x^0=x^0$, the exact recurrence is
$$y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
In positive-dimensional spaces the proximal maps are everywhere single-valued
by [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; in a
zero-dimensional space its sole input and output are the zero vector, so that
proximal call is single-valued directly. The proper closed convexity of $g^*$
follows from [[lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-convex]]. A finite implementation
uses finite call caps and advances an iterate only after both exact proximal
outputs are certified; otherwise it returns **prox-call-failed** or
**prox-cap-exhausted** and makes no convergence claim for that run.

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

Fix a field $F$. The **validated CSR matrix-vector product** takes integer
dimension candidates $m,n$, integer arrays $r,c$, a value array $v$ of elements
of $F$, and a vector candidate $x$ of elements of $F$. All input arrays are
finite; write $s=\operatorname{length}(v)$.

1. If $m\notin\mathbb N$, $n\notin\mathbb N$,
   $\operatorname{length}(r)\ne m+1$,
   $\operatorname{length}(c)\ne s$, or
   $\operatorname{length}(x)\ne n$, return the status `invalid-dimension`.
2. For $i=0,\ldots,m$, check that $r_i\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$; return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails. Check $r_0=0$ and $r_m=s$, and for each
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$ check $r_i\le r_{i+1}$; return `invalid-index` if any
   check fails. For each $t=0,\ldots,s-1$, check $0\le c_t<n$ and return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails.
3. Initialize $y_i=0_F$ for $0\le i<m$. For each row
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$, and then each stored index
   $t=r_i,\ldots,r_{i+1}-1$, update
   $$y_i\gets y_i+v_t x_{c_t}.$$
4. Return the status `ok` together with $y\in F^m$.

For valid CSR data this uses exact field operations. Validation examines only
finite arrays, and the row intervals partition the $s$ stored entries, so the
specified loops are bounded. This procedure makes no floating-point rounding,
backward-stability, convergence, runtime, or memory-bandwidth claim.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let a valid CSR record represent
$A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, and let $x=(x_j)_{j<n}\in F^n$. Define
$(Ax)_i:=\sum_{j<n}A_{ij}x_j$, the usual matrix-vector product from
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Then the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] returns `ok` with output
$Ax$ in exact field arithmetic.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, and let a valid CSR record have
$s$ stored entries. Its input arrays use exactly $s$ field-value slots, $s$
integer column-index slots, and $m+1$ integer row-pointer slots, for a total of
$2s+m+1$ data slots. On valid input, the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] performs exactly $s$ field
multiplications, $s$ field additions, and $m$ zero initializations. Its index
validation and loop-control work is $O(m+s+1)$. Counting the CSR arrays and
returned output but excluding the supplied vector $x$ and constant-size
workspace, it uses exactly $2s+2m+1$ data slots, hence $O(m+s+1)$ slots; for
$m\ge1$ this is $O(m+s)$. Here $O(g)$ means bounded by $Cg$ for a constant $C$ independent of
the dimensions and input values.

For a square record of order $m\ge1$ with at least one stored entry in each
row, $s\ge m$, so the work and storage are $O(s)$. For a canonical record as defined in
[[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]], $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$;
without that convention, the cost is in terms of stored entries, not
$\operatorname{nnz}(A)$. These are arithmetic, index, and storage counts, not
runtime, memory-bandwidth, convergence, or factorization-cost bounds.
